大久保一蔵.note: Ōkubo Toshimichi (1830–1878), the Satsuma statesman who, with Saigō and Kido, drove the Restoration and then built the Meiji state; Ichizō was his earlier name. He was assassinated in 1878.

月真院.note: A sub-temple of Kōdai-ji; the Goryō-eji made it their headquarters, whence they were called the Kōdai-ji party.

ch37.anchor: an Edo foot-guard permanently stationed in the city
ch37.note: An okachi was a foot-soldier retainer of the shogun, the lowest rank of direct vassal, who went on foot where mounted men rode; jōfu means his post kept him permanently in Edo rather than rotating to a lord’s home province. Oyuki is thus of low but genuine Edo samurai stock — the source of the crisp, unsoftened Edo speech that so draws Toshizō.

That Satsuma’s two coming giants, Ōkubo and Nakamura Hanjirō (Kirino), personally cultivated Itō’s little band measures how seriously Satsuma took it: not as ideological friends but as a ready-made strike force inside Kyoto, to be spent when the day came. Historically grounded.

ch37.anchor: a captain of a Great-Guard unit
ch37.note: The ōgoban, the Great Guard, was one of the shogunate’s standing military corps of hatamoto. In the sixth month of 1867 the whole Shinsengumi was taken into direct shogunal service and its leaders given Great-Guard rank — Kondō as a unit commander, Hijikata as a captain. For men born to farming families it was a startling rise, and it is the ‘risen in the world’ that Oyuki gently needles him about. Historically accurate.

ch37.anchor: would have looked down on the samurai of the domains
ch37.note: The distinction is between a jikisan or direct retainer of the shogun (see ch33) and a baishin, a ‘rear-vassal’ — the retainer of some daimyō, and so only the shogun’s vassal’s vassal. Even a common Shinsengumi trooper, now a direct retainer, outranked in theory the samurai of the great domains; the lowest of them fell below omemie, the privilege of being received in the shogun’s presence.

Mokuroku, ‘the catalogue,’ was a middle license in a sword school, above the beginner’s kirigami and below full menkyō; it certified that the pupil had been shown the school’s recorded techniques. Toshizō’s doctor-brother had reached it as a boy under Kondō’s adoptive father.

Rai San’yō (1780–1832), poet and historian, whose Nihon Gaishi (see ch30) shaped the loyalist imagination of the age; to write ‘in the manner of San’yō’ is to write Chinese-style verse in his admired, vigorous mode.

Tatami-iwashi: tiny whitebait spread in a lattice and dried into a thin, crackling sheet, toasted and eaten as a relish — a homely Edo food. That Oyuki asks for it, and colors as she does, is the whole of her homesickness in one word, and it is her Edo-ness Toshizō loves.
